rationale:
The supplied proof has four separable mathematical parts, and each child below is one of them.
- The current-to-measure bridge (parent Step 1): a finite-mass current on ℝ^P has a finite mass measure that equals massOn on every open ball. Only this part uses Submission.iwl_restriction_theory.
- Weak compactness on one closed ball with the closed-set portmanteau inequality (Steps 2a and 3; Simon Ch. 1, 4.16 compact form). This is a pure measure-theory fact.

(ii) ind_md_diagonal_weak_subseq gives φ and (ν_R).
(iii) Apply ind_md_ae_closedBall_growth to every ν_R and combine with ae_all_iff, giving a single Hⁿ-null exceptional set.
(iv) For a good x take R := ⌈‖x‖⌉₊ + 1, (C, r₁) for ν_R, and r₀ := min(r₁, 1). For r ∈ (0, r₀), B̄_r(x) ⊆ B̄_R(0) and limsup_j μ_{φ j}(B̄_r(x)) ≤ ν_R(B̄_r(x)) < ofReal(C rⁿ). subproblems.title: Finite mass measure of a finite-mass current, agreeing with local mass on open balls
subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ and let T ∈ D_n(ℝ^P) (T : GeometricCurrentOn univ n on ℝ^P = Eucl P) have finite mass M(T) = T.mass < ∞. Then there is a measure μ on ℝ^P with μ(ℝ^P) ≤ M(T) and μ(B_r(x)) = M_{B_r(x)}(T) (= T.massOn (ball x r)) for every x ∈ ℝ^P and every r ∈ ℝ, where B_r(x) is the open ball (empty when r ≤ 0).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (T : GeometricCurrentOn (univ : Set (Eucl P)) n), T.mass < ∞ → ∃ μ : Measure (Eucl P), μ univ ≤ T.mass ∧ ∀ (x : Eucl P) (r : ℝ), μ (ball x r) = T.massOn (ball x r)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Step 1, (1a) and (1b), of the parent proof of ind_mass_density_bound, specialized to one current.

Conventions. ℝ^P := Eucl P. M_W(T) := T.massOn W for W ⊆ ℝ^P. M(T) := T.mass, which by definition (GeometricCurrentOn.mass) is M_{ℝ^P}(T) = T.massOn univ. For W ⊆ ℝ^P, 'W ⊂⊂ ℝ^P' means CompactlyContainedOpen W univ: W is open, closure W is compact, and closure W ⊆ univ.

1. Local finiteness. Let W ⊆ ℝ^P. Since W ⊆ univ, monotonicity of the local mass in the support region (GeometricCurrentOn.massOn_mono) gives M_W(T) ≤ M_{univ}(T) = M(T) < ∞. In particular M_W(T) < ∞ for every W ⊂⊂ ℝ^P.

2. Mass measure. Apply the third conjunct (R2) of the comparator-accepted declaration Submission.iwl_restriction_theory with P, k := n, U := univ (open by isOpen_univ), X := T and the local finiteness from step 1. It gives a measure μ on ℝ^P with IsMassMeasure T μ. The two further conclusions, about restrictions, are not needed. By the second component of IsMassMeasure, μ(W) = M_W(T) for every W ⊂⊂ ℝ^P.

3. Balls. Fix x ∈ ℝ^P and r ∈ ℝ.
 - The open ball B_r(x) = ball x r is open (isOpen_ball).
 - Its closure lies in the closed ball B̄_r(x) (closure_ball_subset_closedBall). B̄_r(x) is compact because ℝ^P is a proper metric space (isCompact_closedBall).
 - A closed subset of a compact set is compact (IsCompact.of_isClosed_subset with isClosed_closure), so closure(ball x r) is compact.
 - closure(ball x r) ⊆ univ trivially.
 Hence ball x r ⊂⊂ ℝ^P; this also holds when r ≤ 0, where the ball is empty. Step 2 gives μ(ball x r) = M_{ball x r}(T). This is the second conclusion.

4. Total mass. The balls B_k(0), k ∈ ℕ, increase with k (ball_subset_ball, since k ≤ k′ implies (k : ℝ) ≤ k′), and their union is ℝ^P (iUnion_ball_nat). By continuity of measure along monotone unions (Monotone.measure_iUnion), μ(ℝ^P) = μ(⋃_k B_k(0)) = sup_k μ(B_k(0)). For each k, steps 3 and 1 give μ(B_k(0)) = M_{B_k(0)}(T) ≤ M(T). Hence μ(ℝ^P) ≤ M(T), the first conclusion.
 Lean remark: rewrite only the measured set, for example with calc μ univ = μ (⋃ k : ℕ, ball (0 : Eucl P) k) := by rw [iUnion_ball_nat]. A global rewrite of univ also hits the current's domain inside T.mass and fails with a motive error.

5. By steps 3 and 4, μ has both required properties. ∎
proof_key_steps: For every W, M_W(T) ≤ M(T) < ∞ (massOn_mono), so T has locally finite mass.
Submission.iwl_restriction_theory (R2) with U = univ gives μ with IsMassMeasure T μ, i.e. μ(W) = M_W(T) for every W ⊂⊂ ℝ^P.
Every open ball is ⊂⊂ ℝ^P (its closure lies in a compact closed ball), so μ(ball x r) = M_{ball x r}(T).
μ(ℝ^P) = sup_k μ(B_k(0)) = sup_k M_{B_k(0)}(T) ≤ M(T) (continuity from below along iUnion_ball_nat).

subproblems.title: Weak subsequential compactness of bounded measures on one closed ball, with the closed-set portmanteau inequality
subproblems.statement: Let P, R ∈ ℕ and let μ_j (j ∈ ℕ) be measures on ℝ^P = Eucl P with sup_j μ_j(ℝ^P) < ∞. Then there are a strictly increasing χ : ℕ → ℕ and a measure ν on ℝ^P with ν(ℝ^P) < ∞ such that every closed set F ⊆ ℝ^P with F ⊆ B̄_R(0) = closedBall 0 R satisfies limsup_{i→∞} μ_{χ(i)}(F) ≤ ν(F).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P R : ℕ) (μ : ℕ → Measure (Eucl P)), (⨆ j, μ j univ) < ∞ → ∃ (χ : ℕ → ℕ) (ν : Measure (Eucl P)), StrictMono χ ∧ ν univ < ∞ ∧ ∀ F : Set (Eucl P), IsClosed F → F ⊆ closedBall 0 (R : ℝ) → limsup (fun i => μ (χ i) F) atTop ≤ ν F
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Steps (2a) and 3 of the parent proof of ind_mass_density_bound, applied to one fixed R and the given sequence. Step (2a) is compactness of the measures on the ball K_R (Simon Ch. 1, 4.16, compact metrizable form); Step 3 is the closed-set portmanteau inequality.

Conventions. ℝ^P := Eucl P and K := B̄_R(0) = closedBall (0 : ℝ^P) (R : ℝ). K also denotes the subtype {y // y ∈ K}, with the subspace topology and the subtype σ-algebra. ι : K → ℝ^P is the inclusion Subtype.val. Measures take values in [0, ∞].

1. A real bound. Let L := sup_j μ_j(ℝ^P) < ∞ and Λ := L.toNNReal ∈ ℝ≥0. Since L ≠ ∞, coercing Λ back to [0, ∞] gives L (ENNReal.coe_toNNReal). So μ_j(ℝ^P) ≤ L = Λ for every j (le_iSup).

2. The compact space K.
 - K is compact (isCompact_closedBall), so the subtype K is a compact space (isCompact_iff_compactSpace).
 - It is metrizable as a subspace of a metric space, and its σ-algebra is Borel (Subtype.borelSpace).
 - It is nonempty because 0 ∈ K (R ≥ 0, mem_closedBall_self).
 - K is closed (isClosed_closedBall), hence measurable, so ι is a measurable embedding (MeasurableEmbedding.subtype_coe).
 Consequently (m.comap ι)(S) = m(ι(S)) for every measure m on ℝ^P and every S ⊆ K (MeasurableEmbedding.comap_apply).

3. Finite measures on K. For each j put m_j := μ_j.comap ι. By step 2, m_j(K) = μ_j(ι(univ)) ≤ μ_j(ℝ^P) ≤ Λ < ∞. So m_j is a finite measure on K, i.e. an element of FiniteMeasure K, with mass(m_j) ≤ Λ. To get this, compare in [0, ∞] via FiniteMeasure.ennreal_mass and cast back to ℝ≥0.

4. Compactness. Apply Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.finiteMeasure_tendsto_subseq_of_compact_metrizable (Poincare/SimonGMT/Chapter01/CompactMetrizableCompactness.lean) to the sequence (m_j)_j in FiniteMeasure K with the bound C := Λ. Its hypotheses hold: K is a nonempty compact metrizable Borel space and all masses are ≤ Λ. It gives a strictly increasing χ : ℕ → ℕ and ν̃ ∈ FiniteMeasure K with m_{χ(i)} → ν̃ as i → ∞ in the weak (narrow) topology of FiniteMeasure K.

5. The limit measure. Define ν := (ν̃ regarded as a measure on K).map ι, a measure on ℝ^P. Since ι is measurable (measurable_subtype_coe), ν(B) = ν̃(ι⁻¹(B)) for every measurable B ⊆ ℝ^P (Measure.map_apply). In particular ν(ℝ^P) = ν̃(univ) < ∞, because ν̃ is a finite measure (measure_lt_top).

6. Portmanteau. Let F ⊆ ℝ^P be closed with F ⊆ K. Then ι⁻¹(F) is closed in K (IsClosed.preimage with continuous_subtype_val). K is pseudo-metrizable, so the HasOuterApproxClosed instance applies, and K is an OpensMeasurableSpace because it is Borel. Mathlib's MeasureTheory.FiniteMeasure.limsup_measure_closed_le_of_tendsto (Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/Portmanteau.lean), applied to the convergence of step 4 and the closed set ι⁻¹(F), gives limsup_i m_{χ(i)}(ι⁻¹(F)) ≤ ν̃(ι⁻¹(F)).

7. Back to ℝ^P. For every i:
 m_{χ(i)}(ι⁻¹(F)) = μ_{χ(i)}(ι(ι⁻¹(F))) (step 2)
 = μ_{χ(i)}(F ∩ K) (Subtype.image_preimage_coe)
 = μ_{χ(i)}(F) (F ⊆ K, inter_eq_right).
 Also ν̃(ι⁻¹(F)) = ν(F) by step 5, since F is closed and hence measurable. Substituting into step 6 gives limsup_i μ_{χ(i)}(F) ≤ ν(F).

8. Conclusion. χ is strictly increasing (step 4), ν(ℝ^P) < ∞ (step 5), and limsup_i μ_{χ(i)}(F) ≤ ν(F) for every closed F ⊆ B̄_R(0) (step 7). ∎

Implementation remark. The statement needs only the frozen imports. The proof also needs the imports Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.CompactMetrizableCompactness and Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Measure.Portmanteau; accepted Submission versions already add SimonGMT imports. A Lean proof following steps 1–8 (about 40 lines) was compiled against the frozen project using only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
proof_key_steps: K = closedBall 0 R is a nonempty compact metrizable Borel subtype, and ι = Subtype.val is a measurable embedding, so (m.comap ι)(S) = m(ι S).
m_j := μ_j.comap ι ∈ FiniteMeasure K with mass ≤ Λ.
SimonGMT finiteMeasure_tendsto_subseq_of_compact_metrizable: m_{χ(i)} → ν̃ weakly for some strictly increasing χ.
ν := ν̃.map ι is a finite measure on ℝ^P with ν(B) = ν̃(ι⁻¹B).
Portmanteau (FiniteMeasure.limsup_measure_closed_le_of_tendsto) on K for the closed set ι⁻¹F, with m_{χ(i)}(ι⁻¹F) = μ_{χ(i)}(F) and ν̃(ι⁻¹F) = ν(F).

subproblems.title: Diagonal subsequence with closed-set limsup bounds on every ball B̄_R(0)
subproblems.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ and let μ_j (j ∈ ℕ) be measures on ℝ^P = Eucl P with sup_j μ_j(ℝ^P) < ∞. Then there are a strictly increasing φ : ℕ → ℕ and measures ν_R (R ∈ ℕ) on ℝ^P, with ν_R(ℝ^P) < ∞ for every R, such that for every R ∈ ℕ and every closed set F ⊆ ℝ^P with F ⊆ B̄_R(0) = closedBall 0 R: limsup_{j→∞} μ_{φ(j)}(F) ≤ ν_R(F).
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (μ : ℕ → Measure (Eucl P)), (⨆ j, μ j univ) < ∞ → ∃ (φ : ℕ → ℕ) (ν : ℕ → Measure (Eucl P)), StrictMono φ ∧ (∀ R, ν R univ < ∞) ∧ ∀ (R : ℕ) (F : Set (Eucl P)), IsClosed F → F ⊆ closedBall 0 (R : ℝ) → limsup (fun j => μ (φ j) F) atTop ≤ ν R F
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Steps (2b), (2c) and 3 of the parent proof of ind_mass_density_bound: nested subsequences over R = 0, 1, 2, … and the diagonal φ(j) = (χ_0∘⋯∘χ_j)(j). Here the portmanteau limsup inequality is carried along the diagonal instead of weak convergence. The inequality passes to subsequences, so this gives the same conclusion without re-deriving convergence.

Conventions. ℝ^P := Eucl P. Measures take values in [0, ∞]. limsup means Filter.limsup along atTop. Every strictly increasing χ : ℕ → ℕ satisfies χ(k) ≥ k for all k (StrictMono.id_le), and compositions of strictly increasing maps are strictly increasing (StrictMono.comp).

1. One extraction step. Let R ∈ ℕ and ψ : ℕ → ℕ be arbitrary. Each μ_{ψ(i)}(ℝ^P) is one of the μ_j(ℝ^P), so sup_i μ_{ψ(i)}(ℝ^P) ≤ sup_j μ_j(ℝ^P) < ∞ (iSup_le, le_iSup). Apply the sibling theorem Submission.ind_md_closedBall_weak_subseq to P, R and the sequence i ↦ μ_{ψ(i)}. It gives a strictly increasing χ_{R,ψ} : ℕ → ℕ and a measure ν_{R,ψ} with ν_{R,ψ}(ℝ^P) < ∞ and limsup_i μ_{ψ(χ_{R,ψ}(i))}(F) ≤ ν_{R,ψ}(F) for every closed F ⊆ B̄_R(0). By choice, fix such χ_{R,ψ} and ν_{R,ψ} for every pair (R, ψ) (Lean: choose).

2. Nested subsequences. Define p_R : ℕ → ℕ by recursion on R: p_0 := id and p_{R+1} := p_R ∘ χ_{R,p_R} (Lean: Nat.rec; both defining equations hold by rfl). By induction on R every p_R is strictly increasing: id is, and p_{R+1} is a composition of the strictly increasing maps p_R and χ_{R,p_R}. Put ν_R := ν_{R,p_R}. Step 1 for the pair (R, p_R) gives ν_R(ℝ^P) < ∞. Since p_R(χ_{R,p_R}(i)) = p_{R+1}(i), it also gives
 (∗) limsup_i μ_{p_{R+1}(i)}(F) ≤ ν_R(F) for every closed F ⊆ B̄_R(0).

3. Tails. For all R, d ∈ ℕ there is a strictly increasing g : ℕ → ℕ with p_{R+1+d} = p_{R+1} ∘ g. Proof by induction on d. For d = 0 take g := id. If p_{R+1+d} = p_{R+1} ∘ g, then
 p_{R+1+(d+1)} = p_{(R+1+d)+1} = p_{R+1+d} ∘ χ_{R+1+d, p_{R+1+d}} = p_{R+1} ∘ (g ∘ χ_{R+1+d, p_{R+1+d}}),
 and g ∘ χ_{R+1+d, p_{R+1+d}} is strictly increasing.

4. The diagonal. Define φ(j) := p_{j+1}(j), which is (χ_0 ∘ ⋯ ∘ χ_j)(j) in the parent's notation. For every j, φ(j+1) = p_{j+2}(j+1) = p_{j+1}(χ_{j+1,p_{j+1}}(j+1)), and χ_{j+1,p_{j+1}}(j+1) ≥ j + 1 > j. Since p_{j+1} is strictly increasing, φ(j+1) > p_{j+1}(j) = φ(j). Hence φ is strictly increasing (strictMono_nat_of_lt_succ).

5. Eventual subsequence property. Let R ≤ j. Step 3 with d := j − R gives a strictly increasing g with p_{j+1} = p_{R+1+(j−R)} = p_{R+1} ∘ g. So φ(j) = p_{R+1}(i) with i := g(j) ≥ j.

6. Comparison of limsups. Fix R and a closed F ⊆ B̄_R(0), and put a(k) := μ_k(F) ∈ [0, ∞]. In the complete lattice [0, ∞], limsup_j b(j) = inf_N sup_{j ≥ N} b(j) (limsup_eq_iInf_iSup_of_nat). Fix N. For every j ≥ max(N, R), step 5 gives i ≥ j ≥ N with a(φ(j)) = a(p_{R+1}(i)) ≤ sup_{i′ ≥ N} a(p_{R+1}(i′)). Hence
 limsup_j a(φ(j)) ≤ sup_{j ≥ max(N,R)} a(φ(j)) ≤ sup_{i ≥ N} a(p_{R+1}(i)).
 Taking the infimum over N gives limsup_j a(φ(j)) ≤ limsup_i a(p_{R+1}(i)).

7. Conclusion. For every R and every closed F ⊆ B̄_R(0), step 6 and (∗) give limsup_j μ_{φ(j)}(F) ≤ limsup_i μ_{p_{R+1}(i)}(F) ≤ ν_R(F). With step 4 (φ is strictly increasing) and step 2 (ν_R(ℝ^P) < ∞), φ and (ν_R)_{R∈ℕ} satisfy the statement. ∎

Implementation remark. A Lean proof of exactly this argument (about 55 lines), taking the frozen type of ind_md_closedBall_weak_subseq as a hypothesis, was compiled against the frozen project using only the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.
proof_key_steps: For each R and index map ψ, the sibling ind_md_closedBall_weak_subseq applied to (μ_{ψ(i)})_i gives χ_{R,ψ} and ν_{R,ψ}; choose them for all (R, ψ).
Nested maps p_0 = id and p_{R+1} = p_R ∘ χ_{R,p_R} are strictly increasing; ν_R := ν_{R,p_R} satisfies ν_R(ℝ^P) < ∞ and limsup_i μ_{p_{R+1}(i)}(F) ≤ ν_R(F).
Tails: p_{R+1+d} = p_{R+1} ∘ g with g strictly increasing (induction on d).
The diagonal φ(j) = p_{j+1}(j) is strictly increasing.
For j ≥ R, φ(j) = p_{R+1}(i) with i ≥ j, so limsup_j μ_{φ(j)}(F) ≤ limsup_i μ_{p_{R+1}(i)}(F) ≤ ν_R(F) (via limsup_eq_iInf_iSup_of_nat).

subproblems.title: Hⁿ-a.e. n-dimensional small-ball growth bound for a finite measure
subproblems.statement: Let P, n ∈ ℕ and let ν be a measure on ℝ^P = Eucl P with ν(ℝ^P) < ∞. Then for Hⁿ-a.e. x ∈ ℝ^P (Hⁿ = μHE[n]) there are C ∈ ℝ and r₀ > 0 with ν(B̄_r(x)) < ENNReal.ofReal(C·rⁿ) for every r ∈ (0, r₀), where B̄_r(x) = closedBall x r.
subproblems.lean_statement: ∀ (P n : ℕ) (ν : Measure (Eucl P)), ν univ < ∞ → ∀ᵐ x ∂(μHE[n] : Measure (Eucl P)), ∃ C r₀ : ℝ, 0 < r₀ ∧ ∀ r ∈ Ioo (0 : ℝ) r₀, ν (closedBall x r) < ENNReal.ofReal (C * r ^ n)
subproblems.natural_proof:
Source: Steps 4 and (5a) of the parent proof of ind_mass_density_bound: Simon Ch. 1, Theorem 3.3 with t = ∞, followed by unpacking the finite upper density.

Conventions. ℝ^P := Eucl P and Hⁿ := μHE[n]. ω_n := realUnitBallVolume n = ENNReal.ofReal(π^{n/2}/Γ(n/2 + 1)) (realUnitBallVolume_eq). For x ∈ ℝ^P and r ∈ ℝ, q_x(r) := dimensionalDensityQuotient ν.toOuterMeasure n univ x r = ν(univ ∩ B̄_r(x)) / (ω_n · ENNReal.ofReal(r)^(n:ℝ)). Θ(x) := dimensionalUpperDensity ν.toOuterMeasure n univ x = limsup_{r→0+} q_x(r), the limsup along 𝓝[>] 0, a value in [0, ∞].

1. The infinite-density set is Hⁿ-null. Let A := {x ∈ ℝ^P : Θ(x) = ∞}. Apply the comparator-accepted declaration Submission.rectifiability_density_comparison with P, n, ν, A, V := univ (open) and t := ∞. Its hypotheses hold because A ⊆ univ and ∞ ≤ Θ(x) for every x ∈ A. It gives ∞ · Hⁿ(A) ≤ ν(ℝ^P) < ∞. If Hⁿ(A) ≠ 0, then ∞ · Hⁿ(A) = ∞ (ENNReal.top_mul), contradicting ν(ℝ^P) < ∞. Hence Hⁿ(A) = 0. The comparison theorem allows arbitrary, possibly non-measurable, A, and Hⁿ(A) is the outer measure.

2. Almost-everywhere finiteness. By ae_iff, '∀ᵐ x ∂Hⁿ, Θ(x) < ∞' means Hⁿ({x : ¬ Θ(x) < ∞}) = 0. That set is {x : Θ(x) = ∞} = A (not_lt, top_le_iff). By step 1, Θ(x) < ∞ for Hⁿ-a.e. x. It remains to prove the conclusion for each fixed x with Θ(x) < ∞.

3. Small radii. Fix x with Θ(x) < ∞ and put b := Θ(x) + 1. Then b < ∞ (ENNReal.add_ne_top) and Θ(x) < b (ENNReal.lt_add_right). Since limsup_{r→0+} q_x(r) = Θ(x) < b, eventually in 𝓝[>] 0 we have q_x(r) < b (eventually_lt_of_limsup_lt; the boundedness side condition is automatic in the complete lattice [0, ∞]). By mem_nhdsGT_iff_exists_Ioo_subset there is r₀ > 0 with q_x(r) < b for every r ∈ (0, r₀).

4. The constant ω_n. π^{n/2} > 0 (Real.rpow_pos_of_pos, Real.pi_pos) and Γ(n/2 + 1) > 0 (Real.Gamma_pos_of_pos). So π^{n/2}/Γ(n/2 + 1) > 0 and ω_n ≠ 0 (ENNReal.ofReal_eq_zero). Also ω_n ≠ ∞ because ofReal is finite.

5. Let r ∈ (0, r₀) and d := ω_n · ENNReal.ofReal(r)^(n:ℝ). Since n is a natural number and r ≥ 0, ENNReal.ofReal(r)^(n:ℝ) = ENNReal.ofReal(r)^n = ENNReal.ofReal(rⁿ) (ENNReal.rpow_natCast, ENNReal.ofReal_pow). As rⁿ > 0, ENNReal.ofReal(rⁿ) ∈ (0, ∞), so d ≠ 0 and d ≠ ∞. Moreover ν.toOuterMeasure(univ ∩ B̄_r(x)) = ν(B̄_r(x)) (univ_inter, Measure.coe_toOuterMeasure). So q_x(r) = ν(B̄_r(x))/d < b, and ENNReal.div_lt_iff (with d ≠ 0 and d ≠ ∞) gives ν(B̄_r(x)) < b · d.

6. Real constant. Put C := b.toReal · ω_n.toReal ∈ ℝ. Since b and ω_n are finite, b = ENNReal.ofReal(b.toReal) and ω_n = ENNReal.ofReal(ω_n.toReal) (ENNReal.ofReal_toReal). All real factors are nonnegative, so ENNReal.ofReal_mul gives
 b · d = ENNReal.ofReal(b.toReal) · (ENNReal.ofReal(ω_n.toReal) · ENNReal.ofReal(rⁿ)) = ENNReal.ofReal(b.toReal · (ω_n.toReal · rⁿ)) = ENNReal.ofReal(C · rⁿ).
 Hence ν(B̄_r(x)) < ENNReal.ofReal(C · rⁿ) for every r ∈ (0, r₀).

7. By step 2, the set of x where steps 3–6 apply has Hⁿ-null complement. So for Hⁿ-a.e. x there are C ∈ ℝ and r₀ > 0 as required. ∎
